title: Abelard and Heloise
hook: a teacher who asked yes-and-no questions, and a brilliant abbess with her own theology
carry: by doubting we come to inquiry

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm's argument, made inside a prayer. Your line was greater than can be thought.

A boy is missing. His parents search the city, and when they finally find him, he's in the temple, among the teachers. Luke says he was "both hearing them, and asking them questions." That boy is Jesus. Much later, a teacher in Paris named Peter Abelard points to this very scene to defend something risky: asking questions about the faith out loud. And among the people he taught was a young woman with a mind of her own, named Heloise.

Abelard made a strange book called Sic et Non, Latin for yes and no. He gathered sayings from the church fathers on one question after another, and set them side by side where they seemed to disagree. Yes, says one teacher. No, says another. He didn't settle the questions for his readers. In the preface, he gives reasons the fathers might seem to clash: a word used in different senses, a saying wrongly credited, a copy made badly, a teacher who changed his mind. Then comes today's line. By doubting, Abelard writes, we come to inquiry, and by inquiring we perceive the truth. And he points to Jesus himself: "Seek, and ye shall find." His own story was not peaceful. His love affair with Heloise ended in scandal and a violent attack on him, and both of them entered religious life. Some of his teaching was condemned in his lifetime. Heloise became an abbess, leading a community of nuns. Her letters to Abelard are fierce and honest. She argues that what makes an act good or bad is the intention of the heart, not only the outward deed. She asks him to write a rule fit for women, not one borrowed from men. And she sends him a list of hard questions about puzzling passages in the Bible, asking him to answer them for her nuns. Two people, both convinced that faith can bear honest questions. Christians still disagree about how far doubt should go. But the boy in the temple asked.

Let one real question rise, about faith, about God, about something you were taught and never quite understood. Say it plainly, inside, the way Heloise wrote hers down, and notice how it feels to hold a question without forcing it closed. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is.
Abelard and Heloise. A teacher who set the fathers' yes and no side by side, and an abbess with her own sharp theology, both sure that honest questions lead toward truth.
Your line: by doubting we come to inquiry. And by inquiring, Abelard says, we perceive the truth. Day one thousand two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians bring hard questions to Bible studies, classes, pastors and spiritual directors.

notes: The carry line 'by doubting we come to inquiry' paraphrases the Sic et Non prologue (dubitando ad inquisitionem venimus; inquirendo veritatem percipimus); it is spoken without quotation marks. Check that the prologue cites 'Seek, and ye shall find' and the boy Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:46); the script relies on both.
'Much later' is the only time reference; no dates given.

Biographical summary deliberately brief: love affair, scandal, 'a violent attack on him' (his castration by men acting for Heloise's uncle Fulbert), both entering religious life; 'some of his teaching was condemned in his lifetime' (councils of Soissons and Sens). Confirm tone and accuracy.
Heloise: intention over deed (her letters), request for a rule for women (letter 6 in the usual numbering), and the Problemata (questions on scripture for the Paraclete nuns). Paraphrased; check.
Fork answer is Abelard's method, not a moral test.

Editor pass: the hook said Heloise 'sat among his own students'; by Abelard's own account he taught her privately as her tutor, so it now says she was 'among the people he taught', and drops 'a brilliant mind' (a judgment) for 'a mind of her own'.
Index calls Heloise 'a brilliant abbess'; the script says 'a mind of her own' and, in the word segment, 'her own sharp theology'; confirm.
